items.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023
items.q: You know I was his producer for a while, I produced six records for him.

ctx.x: Did that make it harder to — harder is not the right word — but often times, as you well know, vocals are overdubbed and you have more control over it so if he’s playing the piano at the same time it’s just another task for the engineer I guess.

You know I was his producer for a while, I produced six records for him. And he didn’t overdub anything. Everything was captured. Nothing was manufactured. But if you listen to his early recordings, you know he tends to make kind of grunting sounds when he’s improvising, a lot of jazz musicians do. But on his first records the engineer could have muted his vocal mic during his solos but didn’t. And he was treated harshly that way because the records would come out and you could hear him. And reviewers commented…
You said in around 1990 during one of your presentations, you have a desire to demystify the world of jazz. Jazz musicians are just like the rest of us only more so. Can you expand on that a tad?

items.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Ben Sidran, in his liner notes

ctx.x: Well, it sounds like a lot.

We’ll do it in half-an-hour. It’s not that much. For Part 3, I’d like to return to some quotes from the past. There’s a 1972 recording called Mose In Your Ear. I thought this was an interesting remark. Ben Sidran, in his liner notes, draws out the comparison between your methods of operation and Thelonious Monk’s methods of operations, which he perceives. There are a couple of things... Amy might have quoted this earlier, and forgive me if I’m repeating it. You said: “It’s all a matter of accuracy,” as far as…
